title: Volcanic Ash and the Zero Threshold
paragraphs: The word ash does more harm than good.
It invites a picture of the soft gray powder left in a fireplace after the wood has burned.
Volcanic ash is none of that, and nothing in it has burned.
It shares almost nothing with soot except a color and a habit of hanging in the air.
A pilot who treats ash as smoke will reason about it wrongly.
An engineer who treats it as pulverized rock thrown to cruising altitude will reason about it correctly.
What a volcano ejects is magma torn apart by its own gas.
Water and carbon dioxide dissolved in the melt come out of solution as the magma rises and the pressure falls, and the bubbles expand until the liquid between them cannot hold together.
The melt shatters.
The fragments cool within seconds, far too quickly for their atoms to settle into the ordered lattice of a crystal, so they are quenched into glass, a liquid structure frozen in place.
Fragments smaller than two millimeters across are called ash by convention.
They are angular, hard, and abrasive enough to scour a windscreen from clear to frosted in minutes.
Size decides how far ash travels.
Coarse fragments fall out near the vent.
The fine tail behaves differently.

A particle ten micrometers across, roughly a seventh the width of a human hair, settles through still air at a few millimeters per second, so a cloud injected into the winds at nine kilometers can drift for days and cross an ocean before gravity takes much of it out.
Aviation's problem lies almost entirely in that fine tail, the part that leaves the volcano's neighborhood and arrives where nobody expects it.
Inside a jet engine the trouble starts with temperature.
Air taken in at the front is compressed and burned with fuel in the combustor, where the gas exceeds 1,400 degrees Celsius before it reaches the turbine.
Silicate glass needs nothing like that much heat to lose its shape.
Depending on its composition, volcanic ash begins to soften and flow near 1,100 degrees.
Ash drawn into the intake passes from cold air into a region hundreds of degrees above its own softening range in well under a second.
It does not burn.
There is nothing in it left to burn.
It melts.
Molten ash does not stay molten.

It is carried into the first stage of the turbine, where the metal is deliberately held cooler than the gas around it by air bled from the compressor and blown out through hundreds of small holes in every vane and blade.
Glass touching those cooler surfaces sticks and freezes onto them.
The cooling holes plug, so the metal beneath runs hotter than it was designed to run.
The deposit also narrows the passage the gas must squeeze through, and a turbine whose throat has been narrowed pushes back against the compressor ahead of it.
The airflow breaks down, the flame goes out, and the engine stops.
The recovery is the strange part, and it is why the two most famous encounters ended with everyone alive.
A dead engine cools.
Glass and metal contract at different rates, the brittle layer cracks and flakes away in the airflow, and a shaft still turning in the wind can be relit.
The procedure this implies runs against instinct: descend out of the cloud, giving up altitude in the dark, wait, and try again.
On 24 June 1982 a British Airways Boeing 747 flying from Kuala Lumpur toward Perth entered ash from Mount Galunggung in Java at night.
The weather radar showed nothing, because such radar is built to detect water droplets and is effectively blind to dry ash.
The crew saw a glow on the leading edges, smelled something acrid in the cabin, and then watched all four engines flame out.
The airplane glided for roughly sixteen minutes and lost about 25,000 feet before the engines relit one at a time.
It landed at Jakarta with a windscreen sandblasted nearly opaque.
On 15 December 1989 a new Boeing 747-400 descending toward Anchorage flew into a cloud from Mount Redoubt that had been reported but had not reached the crew usefully.
All four engines failed again.
The airplane fell about 14,000 feet before the crew got them running and landed safely.
Nobody was hurt.
The repair bill, which included four replaced engines, came to roughly 80 million dollars.
Two aircraft, seven years apart, had shown that a hazard invisible to radar could silence a wide-body at cruise.
The institutional answer took shape from the late 1980s into the 1990s as the International Airways Volcano Watch, run under the International Civil Aviation Organization.
Nine Volcanic Ash Advisory Centres divide the globe between them, at London, Toulouse, Anchorage, Washington, Montreal, Buenos Aires, Darwin, Wellington and Tokyo.
When a volcano erupts, the responsible center issues an advisory: polygons drawn on a chart showing where ash is expected at given flight levels now and at six, twelve and eighteen hours ahead.
The polygons come out of a dispersion model, which is only as good as what it is told about the eruption.
It needs source parameters: the height of the column, the mass leaving the vent each second, and the range of particle sizes.
Only height is observed directly, by ground radar or satellite.
The mass rate is usually inferred from height through an empirical relation in which height rises as roughly the fourth root of the rate.
Read the other way, that relation punishes error: mass goes as the fourth power of height, so a column overestimated by a quarter overstates the ash by nearly a factor of two and a half.
The model then releases millions of notional particles into the winds of a weather forecast and follows them.
Direct observation is thinner than it sounds.
The standard satellite technique compares brightness at two infrared wavelengths near eleven and twelve micrometers.
The difference between the two channels comes out positive over water cloud and negative over ash, which lets an analyst tell one from the other.
The method goes blind when ash lies beneath a meteorological cloud, when ice condenses onto the particles and dresses them as weather, and when the layer is very thin.
It also says little about how much ash sits at any one altitude, because a satellite looks down through a whole column and cannot resolve it into layers.
The rule built on all this was short and, for a long time, unarguable: avoid ash.
Not avoid dense ash, not avoid ash above some stated amount.
Avoid it.
The guidance was written when nobody could say what exposure an engine could survive, and in the absence of a number the only defensible number is zero.
The people who wrote it deserve sympathy.
They had two total power losses, no laboratory data, and a duty not to gamble with passengers.
But a rule of that shape quietly makes a claim it cannot support.
The model produces a field of concentrations fading from thick to nothing, with no edge anywhere in it, and the rule needs an edge.
So an edge was drawn wherever the outermost contour fell, everything inside it forbidden and everything outside clear.

The rule was conservative in the engineer's sense of that word: it moved the whole weight of the uncertainty onto the side of not flying, and left the question of how much ash is too much permanently unasked.
For nearly two decades nobody had much reason to ask it.

Certifying an engine against ash would mean expensive testing with a material that varies from one volcano to the next, in order to publish a number that could mainly expose the manufacturer to blame.
While eruptions closed a thinly flown corner of Alaska or the Pacific for a day or two, the cost of not knowing stayed small, and someone else paid it.
Iceland ended that.
Eyjafjallajokull opened as a quiet flank fissure on 20 March 2010, and on 14 April the activity shifted beneath the summit ice cap.

Meltwater reaching the magma chilled and shattered it violently, producing an unusually large proportion of very fine ash, and the weather that month carried it southeast toward the busiest airspace in the world.
Applying the rule as written, authorities closed most of European airspace from 15 to 23 April.
About 100,000 flights were canceled, more than ten million travelers were stranded, and the industry's own estimate of its losses came to roughly 1.7 billion dollars.
No airplane was damaged, because almost none flew.
The closure achieved what two engine failures had not.
Within days, research aircraft carrying particle counters were flying alongside the plume, and ground-based lidar stations were measuring the ash layers passing over Europe.
Much of the closed airspace turned out to hold concentrations far below anything the accident record suggested was dangerous.
Engine manufacturers, pressed to state a tolerance they had never been obliged to state, produced one.

Within weeks the binary chart had become a graded one: below two milligrams of ash per cubic meter of air, ordinary operations; between two and four, flight permitted with the manufacturer's agreement and added inspections; above four, closed.
Two ideas came with the numbers, and both outlast them.

The first is that what harms an engine is a dose, the concentration multiplied by the minutes spent inside it, so a brief crossing of a thick layer and a long cruise through a thin one are not different in kind.
The second is that an advisory should carry its own uncertainty on its face, which is why centers now run their models repeatedly and publish the spread.
When Grimsvotn erupted in May 2011 with an initial column taller than anything Eyjafjallajokull produced, cancellations ran into the hundreds rather than the hundreds of thousands.
The science had not become certain.
It had become quantitative, which is a different and more useful thing.
The lesson worth keeping is not that the 2010 closure was an overreaction.
It is that a threshold of zero is not the absence of a judgment about risk.
It is a judgment made silently, by people who had not been given the data to make it any other way.

questions.stem: According to the passage, ash particles have the structure of a glass rather than a crystal because
choices: they are ground against one another inside the vent until their edges become rounded
dissolved gas keeps crystals from forming at any temperature
meltwater quenches them at the moment they leave the vent
they are melted a second time inside a jet engine
they cool too fast for their atoms to reach an ordered lattice

proof.quote: far too quickly for their atoms to settle into the ordered lattice of a crystal

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says the fragments cool within seconds, far too quickly for their atoms to settle into the ordered lattice of a crystal, so they freeze as glass. Speed of cooling is the whole reason.
distractorNotes: The passage calls the fragments angular, not rounded, and never mentions grinding inside the vent.
Dissolved gas is what tears the magma apart in paragraph 2. It is not offered as a reason crystals fail to form.
Meltwater appears only in the 2010 account in paragraph 14, where it explains fine fragmentation rather than glassy structure.
Melting inside an engine comes in paragraph 4, long after the particle is already glass.

questions.stem: The passage gives the temperature, in degrees Celsius, at which volcanic ash begins to soften and flow as approximately

proof.quote: begins to soften and flow near 1,100 degrees

questions.why: Paragraph 4 states that, depending on composition, ash begins to soften and flow near 1,100 degrees Celsius. The 1,400 figure in the same paragraph belongs to the gas in the combustor.
distractorNotes: Far too low. Paragraph 4 puts the softening point up near 1,100 degrees.
This is the combustor gas, which paragraph 4 says exceeds 1,400 degrees. That is the number the softening point is contrasted against, not the softening point itself.
No figure this high appears anywhere, and the point of the paragraph is that the engine is already hotter than ash needs.
Paragraph 4 gives one specific number for softening, and it is not this one.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 5, a glass deposit in the first turbine stage does which two things?
choices: Cooling holes become blocked and the gas passage is narrowed
The blades melt outright and the shaft seizes
The fuel supply is contaminated and the flame is put out directly
The compressor blades are worn thin and the intake is choked
The turbine spins faster and overspeeds the shaft

proof.quote: The cooling holes plug
narrows the passage the gas must squeeze through

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says the cooling holes plug, so the metal beneath runs hotter than designed, and the deposit narrows the passage the gas must squeeze through. Those are the two effects named.
distractorNotes: The passage says the metal runs hotter than intended. It never says the blades melt or the shaft seizes.
Fuel appears in paragraph 4 only as what burns in the combustor, and the flame goes out because the airflow breaks down.
Wear on the compressor is not what paragraph 5 describes. The damage there is glass sticking to hot turbine parts.
The paragraph describes the opposite. A narrowed throat chokes the flow until the engine stops.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the weather radar on the 1982 flight showed nothing because
choices: it had been switched off earlier in the flight to save electrical power
ash gives back a signal identical to heavy rain
it is built to detect water droplets and cannot see dry ash
the ash cloud was still below the airplane
the crew were watching the engine instruments instead

proof.quote: built to detect water droplets and is effectively blind to dry ash

questions.why: Paragraph 7 explains that weather radar is designed to detect water droplets and is effectively blind to dry ash. The radar was working. It simply cannot see this hazard.
distractorNotes: Nothing in paragraph 7 says the radar was off. The limitation described is what the radar can detect.
If ash looked like rain, the radar would have shown something. Paragraph 7 says it showed nothing at all.
Paragraph 7 says the airplane entered the ash, so the cloud was not beneath it.
The crew noticed the glow and the smell. The radar limit is stated as a property of the radar, not of their attention.

questions.stem: Under the graded scheme in paragraph 15, flight through air carrying three milligrams of ash per cubic meter is
choices: prohibited outright
treated exactly as ordinary operations
allowed only above a stated flight level
permitted with the manufacturer's agreement and added inspections
permitted only for aircraft fitted with one particular type of engine

proof.quote: between two and four, flight permitted with the manufacturer's agreement and added inspections

questions.why: Paragraph 15 sets ordinary operations below two milligrams per cubic meter and closure above four. Three falls in the middle band, where flight is allowed with the manufacturer's agreement and extra inspections.
distractorNotes: Prohibition begins above four milligrams per cubic meter, and three is below that.
Ordinary operations apply below two milligrams per cubic meter, and three is above that.
The bands in paragraph 15 are set by concentration, not by altitude.
No such restriction appears. The condition named is the manufacturer's agreement, not the engine model.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 2, "quenched" most nearly means
choices: soaked in water so that it cools evenly all the way through
extinguished, the way a flame is put out by smothering
satisfied, the way a thirst is relieved by drinking
hardened by repeated cycles of heating and hammering
cooled so fast that a disordered structure is locked in

proof.quote: quenched into glass, a liquid structure frozen in place

questions.why: In paragraph 2 the word sits between rapid cooling and a liquid structure frozen in place, so it means cooling so fast that the disorder of the melt is trapped rather than resolving into crystals.
distractorNotes: Water appears elsewhere in the passage, but paragraph 2 says the fragments cool in air within seconds.
This is the everyday sense. The paragraph is about cooling, and the passage insists nothing in ash is burning.
A real dictionary sense that has nothing to do with a sentence about atoms failing to reach a crystal lattice.
Repeated heating is the opposite of what happens. The fragment gets one very fast cooling and keeps what it leaves.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 12, "conservative" most nearly means
choices: careful with money and therefore unwilling to pay for engine testing
placing the whole burden of uncertainty on the restrictive side
resistant to new technology of any kind
cautious in a way that is always correct
traditional, in keeping with long established practice

proof.quote: moved the whole weight of the uncertainty onto the side of not flying

questions.why: Paragraph 12 defines the word inside the sentence: the rule moved the whole weight of the uncertainty onto the side of not flying. That is the engineering sense the author is naming.
distractorNotes: The cost of testing is raised in paragraph 13, which is a separate point from what the word means here.
Paragraph 12 is about how a safety margin was set, not about attitudes toward technology.
The paragraph separates caution from this word and argues the rule was not simply correct.
Long practice is not the sense here. The author supplies the meaning in the same sentence.

questions.stem: Paragraph 6 most strongly supports which conclusion about ash damage to an engine?
choices: Some of it can undo itself once the engine stops making heat
It is unlikely to occur if the engine is throttled back in advance
It is permanent, so a damaged engine must be replaced before flight continues
It comes mainly from abrasion rather than from melting
It grows worse the longer an engine is left to cool

proof.quote: A dead engine cools.
the brittle layer cracks and flakes away in the airflow

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says a dead engine cools, the glass and metal contract at different rates, and the brittle layer cracks and flakes away so the engine can be relit. The damage partly reverses itself.
distractorNotes: Throttle setting is never discussed. Paragraph 6 describes what happens after the engines have already failed.
Engines were replaced after the 1989 flight, but paragraph 6 explains why a deposit can shed in flight and allow a relight.
Abrasion damages the windscreen in paragraphs 2 and 7. The engine damage in paragraphs 5 and 6 comes from melted glass.
Paragraph 6 says a cooling engine sheds its deposit, so cooling time helps rather than harms.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about advisory boundaries follows most directly from paragraph 10?
choices: They are measured directly by radar and satellite at each flight level
They are drawn deliberately wider than the model output to add a safety margin
They are recalculated only after an eruption has ended
Particle size has no measurable effect on where the model sends the ash
A small error in column height can shift the forecast ash load sharply

proof.quote: mass goes as the fourth power of height
overstates the ash by nearly a factor of two and a half

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says mass goes as the fourth power of height, so a column overestimated by a quarter overstates the ash by nearly a factor of two and a half. An uncertain input becomes a much more uncertain output.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 10 says only the height is observed directly. The mass and the spread are modeled.
Widening for safety is not described in paragraph 10. The question of where the edge falls comes later, in paragraph 12.
The advisories in paragraph 9 look six, twelve and eighteen hours ahead, so they are issued while the eruption continues.
Particle size is listed in paragraph 10 as one of the source parameters the model requires.

questions.stem: Which best states the central point of the passage?
choices: Volcanic ash is dangerous to aircraft chiefly because it is abrasive enough to blind a crew in flight
Aviation met an unmeasured hazard with a blanket ban until a costly closure forced measurement
Dispersion models are now accurate enough to make ash advisories reliable
The 1982 and 1989 failures show that flying near any volcano is unsafe
Iceland's volcanoes pose a uniquely severe threat to European air travel

proof.quote: left the question of how much ash is too much permanently unasked
The closure achieved what two engine failures had not.
a threshold of zero is not the absence of a judgment about risk

questions.why: The passage moves from what ash is, to what it does inside an engine, to a rule of avoid all ash written without data, to the 2010 closure that forced concentration numbers into existence. That arc is the point.
distractorNotes: Abrasion is real in the passage, but it is one detail. The engine failures and the rule built on them carry the argument.
Paragraph 10 stresses how sensitive the models are to an uncertain input, and paragraph 16 says the science became quantitative rather than certain.
The two flights are used to explain where the rule came from, not to argue that flight near volcanoes is unsafe.
Iceland is the case that forced the change, but nine centers cover the whole globe and the problem is framed as a global one.

questions.stem: The first paragraph serves mainly to
choices: establish that ash clouds are visible to a crew well before they are entered
clear away an everyday association before the real material is described
introduce the two accidents that the rest of the passage explains
argue that pilots are less well informed than engineers about volcanoes
explain why ash is hard to detect from a satellite

proof.quote: The word ash does more harm than good.
It invites a picture of the soft gray powder
will reason about it correctly

questions.why: Paragraph 1 spends its whole length separating volcanic ash from fireplace ash and soot, so that the reader stops picturing something burned and soft before paragraph 2 describes pulverized rock.
distractorNotes: The passage says the opposite in paragraph 7, where the radar showed nothing and the encounter happened at night.
The accidents arrive in paragraphs 7 and 8. The opening is about what ash is and is not.
The pilot and engineer sentences contrast two mental pictures of ash, not the competence of two professions.
Satellite detection is the subject of paragraph 11 and is not raised in the opening.

questions.stem: Which best describes how the passage is organized?
choices: A list of eruptions arranged from earliest to most recent
A comparison of two competing explanations for the engine failures
A single problem stated at the start and then deliberately left unresolved at the end
A substance, then a mechanism, then a rule, then the event that revised it
A history of one regulatory body told through its nine centers

proof.quote: What a volcano ejects is magma torn apart by its own gas.
Inside a jet engine the trouble starts with temperature.
The rule built on all this was short
Iceland ended that.

questions.why: Paragraphs 1 through 3 describe the material, 4 through 6 the mechanism inside an engine, 7 through 13 the accidents and the rule they produced, and 14 through 16 the eruption that forced the rule to be rewritten.
distractorNotes: Eruptions do appear in date order, but they occupy a small part of a passage that moves from substance to mechanism to regulation.
Only one mechanism is offered anywhere: melted silicate glass freezing onto cooler turbine metal.
The closing paragraphs resolve the problem with graded thresholds and the idea of a dose.
The nine centers occupy one paragraph. This is not an institutional history.

questions.stem: The author's attitude in paragraph 12 toward the people who wrote the avoid all ash rule is best described as
choices: openly scornful of their unwillingness to gather evidence
indifferent, since the rule has since been replaced
understanding of their position while critical of what the rule hid
admiring, with no reservations about the rule itself
puzzled that anyone would restrict flight over a hazard they could not see

proof.quote: The people who wrote it deserve sympathy.
quietly makes a claim it cannot support

questions.why: Paragraph 12 says those people deserve sympathy and had a duty not to gamble with passengers, then argues in the same breath that the rule makes a claim it cannot support and leaves a question permanently unasked.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 12 states plainly that these people deserve sympathy and faced a real duty.
Indifference does not fit a paragraph that argues at length about what the rule left unasked.
The sympathy is genuine, but the same paragraph says the rule quietly makes a claim it cannot support.
The author treats the hazard as real throughout and questions only the shape of the rule.

questions.stem: In the final paragraph, the author's attitude toward the 2010 closure is best described as
choices: unwilling to call it a mistake, since the number needed was missing
firmly convinced that it was a clear overreaction by regulators who were too cautious
certain that it prevented a disaster that would otherwise have taken place
neutral, offering the reader no view of the episode at all
regretful that airlines were not consulted before the airspace was closed

proof.quote: not that the 2010 closure was an overreaction
had not been given the data to make it any other way

questions.why: The last paragraph says directly that the lesson worth keeping is not that the closure was an overreaction, and then reframes a threshold of zero as a silent judgment made without data.
distractorNotes: The final paragraph rejects this reading in so many words.
The passage says no airplane was damaged because almost none flew. It does not claim a disaster was averted.
The author does take a position, calling a threshold of zero a judgment made silently.
Consultation is never raised. The gap the author names is data, not process.

questions.stem: The passage presents all of the following as limits on knowing where ash is and how much of it is there EXCEPT
choices: Weather radar returns no signal from dry ash
A satellite cannot separate a column into layers
The mass leaving the vent is inferred rather than measured
Forecast winds are unavailable to the modeling centers
The satellite method fails when ash sits under ordinary cloud

proof.quote: into the winds of a weather forecast
effectively blind to dry ash
cannot resolve it into layers
The mass rate is usually inferred from height
when ash lies beneath a meteorological cloud

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says the model releases its particles into the winds of a weather forecast, so forecast winds are exactly what the centers do have. The other four limits appear in paragraphs 7, 10 and 11.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 7 gives this as the reason the radar showed nothing in 1982.
Paragraph 11 says a satellite looks down through a whole column and cannot resolve layers.
Paragraph 10 says the mass rate is inferred from column height rather than observed.
Paragraph 11 lists ash beneath a meteorological cloud as a case where the method goes blind.

questions.stem: A reader who wanted to find out how air taken from the compressor is used to keep turbine metal cool should look in which paragraph?
choices: Paragraph 2
Paragraph 4
Paragraph 5
Paragraph 9
Paragraph 11

proof.quote: air bled from the compressor and blown out through hundreds of small holes

questions.why: Paragraph 5 is the one that describes air bled from the compressor and blown out through hundreds of small holes in every vane and blade to hold the metal cooler than the gas.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 2 is about how ash forms and what it is made of.
Paragraph 4 gives the temperatures, but the cooling air and the holes appear one paragraph later.
Paragraph 9 covers the advisory centers, not engine hardware.
Paragraph 11 is about satellite detection.
